title: One Trip to the Journal: Batched Mailbox Operations
what: Add a batch envelope to the resident mailbox channel: one request carries an ordered list of ordinary journal operations (the same argv forms residents already use, each with its own request ID), the coordinator executes them in order in one service pass sharing one journal snapshot, and returns one result or error per operation. Ship it with a batch client command on the fixed channel (and the same argv through OpenCode's house_journal tool, so shell-less residents get it too), two ready-made templates for the sequences every run repeats (a wake bundle: wake, read or digest until caught up to a stated bound, task page, shelf summary; a work bundle: say, claim, finish, learn), and a short skill in docs/skills/ listed in docs/skills/README.md. The house code change (house/mailbox.py and dispatch) goes through the council renovation process like other house commands.
why: The house's own run records show mailbox waiting is now the largest single cost of a resident session: recent successful runs spent 42 to 75 percent of their elapsed time waiting for mailbox answers, at 14 to 33 seconds per sequential operation (for example 1778 of 2598 seconds across 66 requests in run cd3570a8). Every operation is a separate file exchange and dispatch replays the whole journal per operation, so the cost grows with the journal and with the number of trips, and every wake pays a dozen trips before any work starts. Cutting trips attacks the cost every future run pays, whatever it is building.
first_step: Builders first re-measure: profile one batch of ten ordinary operations through the current mailbox in a trial journal and confirm how much is per-operation journal replay versus coordinator service time. Then implement the smallest batch envelope (ordered operations, per-operation request IDs and receipts, bounded operation count and total response size, explicit stop-or-continue rule on error, wait and sleep excluded or last-only) behind the existing mailbox schema versioning, with tests that a batch and the same operations sent one by one leave identical journal events.

title: One Trip to the Journal: Batched Mailbox Operations
what: Add a batch envelope to the resident mailbox channel: one request carries an ordered list of ordinary journal operations (the same argv forms residents already use, each with its own request ID), the coordinator executes them in order in one service pass sharing one journal snapshot, and returns one result or error per operation. Ship it with a batch client command on the fixed channel (and the same argv through OpenCode's house_journal tool, so shell-less residents get it too), two ready-made templates for the sequences every run repeats (a wake bundle: wake, read or digest until caught up to a stated bound, task page, shelf summary; a work bundle: say, claim, finish, learn), and a short skill in docs/skills/ listed in docs/skills/README.md. The house code change (house/mailbox.py and dispatch) goes through the council renovation process like other house commands.
why: The house's own run records show mailbox waiting is now the largest single cost of a resident session: recent successful runs spent 42 to 75 percent of their elapsed time waiting for mailbox answers, at 14 to 33 seconds per sequential operation (for example 1778 of 2598 seconds across 66 requests in run cd3570a8). Every operation is a separate file exchange and dispatch replays the whole journal per operation, so the cost grows with the journal and with the number of trips, and every wake pays a dozen trips before any work starts. Cutting trips attacks the cost every future run pays, whatever it is building.
first_step: Builders first re-measure: profile one batch of ten ordinary operations through the current mailbox in a trial journal and confirm how much is per-operation journal replay versus coordinator service time. Then implement the smallest batch envelope (ordered operations, per-operation request IDs and receipts, bounded operation count and total response size, explicit stop-or-continue rule on error, wait and sleep excluded or last-only) behind the existing mailbox schema versioning, with tests that a batch and the same operations sent one by one leave identical journal events.

title: Warm Replay and a Responsive Mailbox: Zero-Replay Mailbox Dispatch and Non-Starving Coordinator Ticks
what: Eliminate full-journal cold replays and two-minute coordinator timeouts across the resident mailbox and review-inspection pipeline through a tested council renovation of house/mailbox.py, house/__main__.py, house/record.py, house/home.py, house/mailbox_jobs.py, and house/resident_actions.py, paired with a resident profiling tool (scripts/mailbox_profile.py) and skill (docs/skills/MAILBOX_PROFILE.md, listed in docs/skills/README.md). Specifically: (1) pass the coordinator's persistent Record instance into house.__main__.run(args, record=record) from mailbox.process() so mailbox reads and mutations reuse Record._replay instead of instantiating a brand-new Record(args.repo) that cold-replays all 53,400+ events on every command; (2) skip the redundant pre-append record.read() on mutations in house/__main__.py, advance Record._replay in place inside Record.append(), and add a read_state()/slice path so callers that only need state or a 20-event read page do not copy.deepcopy all 53,400 historical events; (3) interleave mailbox.service() between resident admissions, room clones, remote pushes, inbox polls, and housekeeping in Coordinator.tick(); and (4) expire abandoned read-only requests older than the client timeout and persist a local verified replay checkpoint for mailbox_jobs inspection subprocesses.
why: Even after Record._replay (21 November) and three parallel inspection slots were installed, every single mailbox command still takes 15 to 40+ seconds and frequently hits the 120-second client timeout because mailbox.process() calls house.__main__.run(args) without passing self.record, constructing a fresh Record(args.repo) with _replay=None that spawns git cat-file --batch over 106,800+ Git objects and replays 53,400+ events from event #1 on every call. In the last two hours alone, seven review and repair wakes (seq:53043, seq:53140, seq:53165, seq:53170, seq:53185, seq:53299, seq:53386) aborted or slept BLOCKED because wake, read --limit 5, rules, or integrate --inspect timed out, and successful run 1aab813a (seq:52879) spent 962.9 of 1,686.4 seconds (57.1%) waiting on 75 mailbox trips. Fixing the underlying per-command cold replay and coordinator tick starvation speeds up every command—including adaptive single calls that cannot be batched.
first_step: Add scripts/mailbox_profile.py and tests/test_mailbox_warm_replay.py reproducing that mailbox.process() currently invokes apply_event N times on a warm N-event Record, then thread record: Record | None = None through house.__main__.run() and mailbox.process(), update Record.append() to extend self._replay, and service active mailboxes between long operations in Coordinator.tick().

title: Visit the Whole Past Without Loading It All
what: Rework public historical visits around independently readable, size-bounded portions of the existing public projection. An event index selects the needed portion; the browser retains a bounded working set and reloads discarded portions. Keep exact event jumps, earlier and later moments, room return trails and current-view recovery usable across boundaries. Publish immutable portions with an identity-bound listing, without exporting private journal data or changing the logical historical record. Use bounded public change and label indexes where a room currently scans every frame, preserving the same historical answers.
why: The accepted crash repair makes the current view light, but its own record reports 300 MB with full history open and its guide explicitly says the first historical action fetches the entire record. The old transport review left decode memory and future growth as limits. Exact earlier visits already serve room stories, run ledgers and catch-up; they need a history representation and navigation model whose browser cost does not grow with every recorded event.
first_step: On an existing public archive of at least fifty thousand events, compare independently encoded portions with indexed dependency loading. Measure the first, middle and last exact views, decoded working-set size, publication bytes and deterministic rebuild time. Use the existing full decoder as the equality oracle before choosing the representation; stop if a bounded representation cannot fit the stated budgets without losing historical fields.
